claim: Mollicutes were recently identified as abundant abdominal endosymbionts in healthy workers of attine fungus-farming leaf-cutting ants.
source: Mollicutes, a widespread class of bacteria associated with animals and plants, were recently identified as abundant abdominal endosymbionts in healthy workers of attine fungus-farming leaf-cutting ants.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Sapountzis et al., 2015; Meirelles et al., 2016) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 are independently acquired symbionts.
source: Reconstructions of their functional significance showed that they are independently acquired symbionts, most likely to decompose excess arginine consistent with the farmed fungal cultivars providing this nitrogen-rich amino-acid in variable quantities.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenomic analysis presented in Figure 1 showing that EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 are not closely related.

claim: EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 decompose excess arginine provided by fungal cultivars.
source: Reconstructions of their functional significance showed that they are independently acquired symbionts, most likely to decompose excess arginine consistent with the farmed fungal cultivars providing this nitrogen-rich amino-acid in variable quantities.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic pathway reconstructions (Figure 2, Figure 5) and gene expression data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: EntAcro1 has special genomic machinery to catabolize citrate/glucose into acetate.
source: One of the symbionts is specific to the leaf-cutting ants and has special genomic machinery to catabolize citrate/glucose into acetate, which appears to deliver direct metabolic energy to the ant workers.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis showing the citrate utilization operon (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and metabolic pathway reconstruction (Figure 2).

claim: Acetate produced by EntAcro1 delivers direct metabolic energy to ant workers.
source: One of the symbionts is specific to the leaf-cutting ants and has special genomic machinery to catabolize citrate/glucose into acetate, which appears to deliver direct metabolic energy to the ant workers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between EntAcro1 abundance and MCT1 expression (Figure 4).

claim: Both EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 have complete phage-defense systems.
source: Unlike other Mollicutes associated with insect hosts, both attine ant strains have complete phage-defense systems, underlining that they are actively maintained as mutualistic symbionts.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis showing Type-I R-M system and CRISPR pathways (Figure 5).

claim: Complete phage-defense systems indicate that EntAcro symbionts are actively maintained as mutualistic symbionts.
source: Unlike other Mollicutes associated with insect hosts, both attine ant strains have complete phage-defense systems, underlining that they are actively maintained as mutualistic symbionts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of costly defense systems and comparison with other Mollicutes.

claim: Bacterial endosymbionts occur in all eukaryotic lineages.
source: Bacterial endosymbionts, defined here as comprising both intra- and extra-cellular symbionts (Bourtzis and Miller, 2006), occur in all eukaryotic lineages and range from parasites to mutualists (Bourtzis and Miller, 2006; Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Endosymbiont genomes tend to evolve faster than those of free-living bacteria.
source: Their genomes tend to evolve faster than those of free-living bacteria (Delaney et al., 2012; Moran et al., 1995) and they often rely on recombination and horizontal gene transfer when their tissue localizations allow frequent DNA exchange with other bacteria, which tends to purge deleterious mutations when effective population sizes are small (Naito and Pawlowska, 2016; Takeuchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Buchnera provides aphids with essential amino acids.
source: Examples are Buchnera (γ-Proteobacteria) providing aphids with essential amino acids (Baumann et al., 1995; Shigenobu et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Wolbachia produces vitamin B for Cimex lectularius bedbugs.
source: Wolbachia (α-Proteobacteria) producing vitamin B for Cimex lectularius bedbugs (Hosokawa et al., 2010; Nikoh et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Baumannia and Sulcia provide sharpshooters with vitamins and amino acids.
source: Baumannia and Sulcia (γ-Proteobacteria) providing sharpshooters (Homalodisca coagulata) with vitamins and amino acids (Wu et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nardonella provides beetles with tyrosine required for cuticle formation.
source: Nardonella (γ-Proteobacteria) providing beetles with tyrosine required for cuticle formation (Anbutsu et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stammera bacteria allow leaf beetles to decompose pectin.
source: Stammera bacteria allowing leaf beetles to decompose pectin (Salem et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nutrient supplementation often drives evolution towards host dependence especially when symbionts are vertically transmitted.
source: A recent comparative analysis confirmed that nutrient supplementation often drives evolution towards host dependence especially when symbionts are vertically transmitted (Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Blochmannia provides amino acid provisioning to Camponotus carpenter ants.
source: Previous studies have documented amino acid provisioning by Blochmannia (γ-Proteobacteria) hosted by Camponotus carpenter ants (Feldhaar et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Bacterial symbionts provision Cephalotes turtle ants with essential amino acids.
source: suggested that bacterial symbionts provision Cephalotes turtle ants with essential amino acids (Hu et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and is presented as a suggestion.

claim: Bacterial symbionts provision Cardiocondyla ants with useful intermediate metabolites.
source: suggested that bacterial symbionts provision Cephalotes turtle ants with essential amino acids (Hu et al., 2018) and Cardiocondyla ants with useful intermediate metabolites (Klein et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and is presented as a suggestion.

claim: Honeybees rely on several specialized gut bacteria for carbohydrate breakdown of ingested pollen and nectar.
source: Honeybees were further suggested to rely on several specialized gut bacteria for carbohydrate breakdown of ingested pollen and nectar (Engel et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and is presented as a suggestion.

claim: Fungus-growing termites have caste-specific microbiomes depending on whether individuals ingest plant material or only farmed fungus.
source: fungus-growing termites were discovered to have caste-specific microbiomes depending on whether individuals ingest plant material (mainly decaying wood) or only farmed fungus (Poulsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Bees and termites rely on gut microbes to provide them with acetate that can cover up to 100% of their metabolic needs.
source: Finally, both bees and termites rely on gut microbes to provide them with acetate that can cover up to 100% of their metabolic needs (Odelson and Breznak, 1983; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The attine fungus-growing ants evolved 55–60 MYA when their ancestor switched from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to an exclusive fungal diet.
source: The leaf-cutting ants are the crown group of the attine fungus-growing ants, a monophyletic tribe that evolved 55–60 MYA when their ancestor switched from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to an exclusive fungal diet (Nygaard et al., 2016; Branstetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fungal cultivars provide ant farmers with specialized hyphal tips (gongylidia) containing mostly carbohydrates and lipids.
source: The evolutionarily derived attine lineages rear fully domesticated and co-adapted fungal cultivars that provide the ant farmers with specialized hyphal tips (gongylidia) containing mostly carbohydrates and lipids that the workers harvest and digest (De Fine Licht et al., 2014; Quinlan and Cherrett, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ant brood is completely dependent on the ingestion of fungal biomass.
source: The ant brood is completely dependent on the ingestion of fungal biomass (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Ant workers cannot ingest solid plant or animal fragments because a sieve in the infrabuccal cavity filters out any particles in excess of ca. 100 µm.
source: However, similar to other ants, they cannot ingest solid plant or animal fragments that they collect to provision their fungus gardens because a sieve in the infrabuccal cavity filters out any particles in excess of ca. 100 µm (Mueller et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Acromyrmex and Atta leaf-cutting ants evolved 15-20 MYA.
source: This obligate reciprocity between cultivation and nutrition facilitated further innovations in the terminal clade of Acromyrmex and Atta leaf-cutting ants, which evolved 15-20 MYA (Nygaard et al., 2016; Branstetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Leaf-cutting ants obtained functionally polyploid cultivars.
source: These two genera obtained functionally polyploid cultivars (Kooij et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Leaf-cutting ants adopted multiple queen-mating so their colonies became genetic chimeras.
source: adopted multiple queen-mating so their colonies became genetic chimeras (Villesen et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Acromyrmex and Atta leaf-cutting ants harbor low-diversity microbiomes, which include Wolbachia (only in Acromyrmex), Mollicutes and hindgut Rhizobiales.
source: Previous studies have shown that Acromyrmex and Atta leaf-cutting ants harbor low-diversity microbiomes, which include Wolbachia (only in Acromyrmex), Mollicutes and hindgut Rhizobiales (Van Borm et al., 2002; Andersen et al., 2012; Sapountzis et al., 2015; Meirelles et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mollicutes can be found as abundant endosymbionts in up to 100% of leaf-cutting ant colonies.
source: Depending on the actual species studied, Mollicutes – tiny bacteria that lack a cell-wall – can often be found as abundant endosymbionts in up to 100% of leaf-cutting ant colonies (Sapountzis et al., 2015; Meirelles et al., 2016; Zhukova et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 are the two most common Mollicutes strains in Panamanian fungus-growing ants.
source: To clarify the functional metabolic properties of attine-associated Mollicutes, we mapped the abundances of the two most common strains, EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 (cf. Sapountzis et al., 2015), in thirteen Panamanian fungus-growing ant species
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The draft genomes of EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 had 758 and 776 coding sequences, respectively.
source: These genomes had 758 and 776 coding sequences, respectively, and genome sizes of less than 0.9 Kb based on the annotation features (Supplementary file 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by genomic data in supplementary files.

claim: EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 belong to the Entomoplasmatales group.
source: This produced nearly identical trees after maximum likelihood (Figure 1) and Bayesian analysis of nucleotide and amino acid sequences (Supplementary file 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and revealed that EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 belong to the Entomoplasmatales group, confirming earlier 16S assignments (Sapountzis et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenomic analysis (Figure 1) and previous 16S data.

claim: EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 are not closely related and thus likely to have been independently acquired as attine ant symbionts.
source: Sister-group relationships showed that EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 are not closely related and thus likely to have been independently acquired as attine ant symbionts.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenomic analysis showing distant relationships (Figure 1).

claim: EntAcro10 is a relatively basal Spiroplasma-like species.
source: EntAcro10 is a relatively basal Spiroplasma-like species, a genus with pathogenic, mutualistic and yet unknown interactions with mostly arthropod hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenomic analysis (Figure 1).

claim: EntAcro1 is sister to the Mesoplasma/Mycoplasma clade.
source: However, EntAcro1 is sister to the Mesoplasma/Mycoplasma clade and relatively similar to one of the very few Entomoplasmatales known to be associated with plant hosts in a clade that otherwise consists of vertebrate pathogens.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenomic analysis (Figure 1).

claim: All Entomoplasmatales are facultative anaerobes because they lack the genes encoding TCA cycle enzymes.
source: Metabolic reconstructions (KEGG) further suggested that all Entomoplasmatales are facultative anaerobes, because they lack the genes encoding TCA cycle enzymes and are thus universally incapable of oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on metabolic pathway reconstruction from genomic data.

claim: EntAcro1 likely lost its aerobic abilities completely because pyruvate dehydrogenase genes are missing.
source: However, EntAcro1 likely lost its aerobic abilities completely because pyruvate dehydrogenase genes are also missing.
evidence: This claim is based on genomic analysis showing absence of specific genes.

claim: Functional gene-similarities were more strongly associated with phylogenomic distances between insect hosts than with phylogenomic distances between bacterial species.
source: Functional gene-similarities were confirmed by Mantel tests showing that the Euclidean dissimilarity matrix of orthogroups was more strongly associated with phylogenomic distances between insect hosts (r2 = 0.298, p=0.036) than with phylogenomic distances between bacterial species (Figure 1; r2 = 0.201, p=0.133)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mantel tests) of genomic data.

claim: Many genes that adapt Entomoplasmatales symbionts to their hosts have been horizontally acquired.
source: suggesting that many genes that adapt Entomoplasmatales symbionts to their hosts have been horizontally acquired.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Mantel test results showing stronger association with host phylogeny than bacterial phylogeny.

claim: EntAcro10 can utilize glycerol from ant host cells and monosaccharides derived from fungus-garden metabolites or juices.
source: We found that EntAcro10 can utilize glycerol from ant host cells and monosaccharides which are likely derived from fungus-garden metabolites or juices (glucose/fructose) ingested during foraging (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on metabolic pathway reconstruction shown in Figure 2.

claim: EntAcro10 has an arginine transporter and metabolic genes indicating it can decompose arginine.
source: We also found an arginine transporter and metabolic genes indicating that EntAcro10 can decompose arginine.
evidence: This claim is based on genomic analysis and pathway reconstruction (Figure 2).

claim: Attine ants lost the ability to synthesize arginine when fungus-farming evolved.
source: This finding is of interest because the attine ants lost the ability to synthesize this nitrogen-rich amino acid (highest nitrogen to carbon ratio of all amino acids) when fungus-farming evolved, so they obtain arginine from the fungal cultivar and potentially also from ingested fruit juice and plant sap in the herbivorous crown-group leaf-cutting ants (Kooij et al., 2014a; Winter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EntAcro1 has a GlcNAc transporter likely importing chitin monomers.
source: First, it has a GlcNAc transporter likely importing chitin monomers, a relatively common metabolic pathway in Mollicutes found in 85 of the 177 genomes that we considered.
evidence: This claim is based on genomic analysis and comparative genomics.

claim: Chitin is one of the most abundant compounds in the ants' fungal diet.
source: The possession of a chitin importer is relevant because chitin is one of the most abundant compounds in the ants' fungal diet (Figure 2)
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about fungal cell wall composition.

claim: EntAcro1 has a rare citrate transporter indicative of a catabolic pathway observed in only four of the 177 available Mollicutes genomes.
source: Second, EntAcro1 has a rather unique citrate transporter indicative of a rare catabolic pathway observed in only four of the 177 available Mollicutes genomes; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Anaerobic citrate fermentation using the citS-citF operon will produce acetate.
source: Anaerobic citrate fermentation, or co-fermentation of glucose/citrate, using the citS-citF operon will produce acetate (Pudlik and Lolkema, 2011; Starrenburg and Hugenholtz, 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on citrate metabolism.

claim: Acetate produced by EntAcro1 is likely imported by eukaryote cells to fuel metabolism.
source: Anaerobic citrate fermentation, or co-fermentation of glucose/citrate, using the citS-citF operon will produce acetate (Pudlik and Lolkema, 2011; Starrenburg and Hugenholtz, 1991), which is likely imported by eukaryote cells to fuel metabolism (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) or stored in the fat body cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on known acetate metabolism in eukaryotes and experimental data (Figure 4).

claim: Leaf-cutting ants can utilize citrate metabolite that they ingest in substantial quantities as plant sap when cutting fresh leaves.
source: The citrate pathway thus appears to reflect that leaf-cutting ants can utilize the citrate metabolite that they are known to ingest in substantial quantities as plant sap when cutting fresh leaves (Littledyke and Cherrett, 1976) and in the form of other juices when drinking from freshly fallen fruit (De Fine Licht and Boomsma, 2010; Evison and Ratnieks, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on leaf-cutting ant foraging behavior.

claim: EntAcro10 was present in most attine species investigated with no significant differences across the entire set of 13 species.
source: EntAcro10 was present in most attine species investigated such that there were no significant differences across the entire set of 13 species (planned contrasts, z = −0.62, p=1.00).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of qPCR data presented in Figure 3.

claim: EntAcro1 was almost exclusively found in the leaf-cutting ants.
source: However, EntAcro1 was almost exclusively found in the leaf-cutting ants (planned contrasts, z = 2.88, p=0.016) with their closest Panamanian relative T. cornetzi and yeast-growing C. rimosus as the only (partial) exceptions.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of qPCR data presented in Figure 3.

claim: EntAcro10 abundances in leaf-cutting ants were lower than EntAcro1 abundances.
source: At the same time EntAcro10 abundances in leaf-cutting ants were lower than EntAcro1 abundances albeit only marginally so (planned contrasts, z = −2.56, p=0.045)(Figure 3A; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of qPCR data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The appearance of EntAcro1 is correlated with changes in the spectrum of substrates that the farming ants provide to their fungus gardens.
source: This pattern implies that the appearance of EntAcro1 is correlated with changes in the spectrum of substrates that the farming ants provide to their fungus gardens (Figure 3B;Figure 3—source data 2)
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis between bacterial abundances and foraging substrate data.

claim: Bacterial abundances and foraging preferences covaried for EntAcro1 but not for EntAcro10.
source: These differences were variably (non)significant per forage category (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but bacterial abundances and foraging preferences generally covaried for EntAcro1 (Mantel test; r2 = 0.447, p=0.012) but not for EntAcro10 (Mantel test; r2 = −0.127, p=0.882).
evidence: This claim is supported by Mantel test statistical analysis.

claim: The derived metabolic pathways of EntAcro1 may have been associated with the expansion of the scale of fungus farming and the adoption of functional herbivory in the leaf-cutting ants.
source: These results suggest that the derived metabolic pathways of EntAcro1 (Figure 2) may have been associated with the expansion of the scale of fungus farming and the adoption of functional herbivory in the leaf-cutting ants.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the correlation between EntAcro1 presence and leaf-cutting ant foraging behavior.

claim: Expression of ftsZ and MCT1 were positively correlated.
source: We found that these variables were positively correlated (ρ = 0.57, p<0.001), suggesting that acetate production by EntAcro1 boosts acetate uptake by the ants who likely convert acetate directly into ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Acetate production by EntAcro1 boosts acetate uptake by the ants who likely convert acetate directly into ATP.
source: We found that these variables were positively correlated (ρ = 0.57, p<0.001), suggesting that acetate production by EntAcro1 boosts acetate uptake by the ants who likely convert acetate directly into ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between bacterial abundance and MCT1 expression.

claim: Conversion of citrate to acetate by the EntAcro1 symbiont would be consistent with leaf-cutting ants sustaining much higher levels of worker activity than phylogenetically more basal attine ants.
source: Conversion of citrate to acetate by the EntAcro1 symbiont would be consistent with the general observation that leaf-cutting ants sustain much higher levels of worker activity, both inside nests and while foraging, than phylogenetically more basal attine ants (Kooij et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is an inference connecting metabolic function to observed behavioral differences, supported by citation.

claim: The arginine transporter was more highly expressed in EntAcro1 cells in the hindgut lumen.
source: Posthoc tests using planned contrasts showed that the arginine transporter was more highly expressed in EntAcro1 cells in the hindgut lumen (planned contrasts: z = 2.09, p=0.044)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The glycerol/DHA transporter was more highly expressed in EntAcro1 cells of the fat body/midgut compartment.
source: while the glycerol/DHA transporter was more highly expressed in EntAcro1 cells of the fat body/midgut compartment (planned contrasts: z = −2.45, p=0.019).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the related Spiroplasma symbionts associated with other insects had the same dual defense system against phage attack as EntAcro1 and EntAcro10.
source: Gene-level comparisons with the other Spiroplasma symbionts showed that none of them had the same dual defense system against phage attack.
evidence: This claim is based on comparative genomic analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Type I R-M system genes were present only in non-pathogenic Mollicutes strains.
source: Type I R-M system genes were present only in non-pathogenic Mollicutes strains, similar to arginine catabolism pathways being restricted to Spiroplasma strains with non-pathogenic host associations, except for the reputedly pathogenic S. apis (Figure 5; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on comparative genomic analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: The CRISPR system was complete only in S. chrysopicola, S.apis, and the two ant associated EntAcro strains.
source: The generally rarer CRISPR system was complete (i.e. both CRISPR repeat/space regions and cas genes being present) only in S. chrysopicola, S.apis, and the two ant associated EntAcro strains.
evidence: This claim is based on comparative genomic analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Spiroplasma-specific phages of the Gokushovirinae were found in the contig bin 'C' of the EntAcro1 symbiont isolated from fecal fluid.
source: We did indeed find Spiroplasma-specific phages of the Gokushovirinae in the contig bin 'C' of the EntAcro1 symbiont (Supplementary file 1C) isolated from fecal fluid.
evidence: This claim is based on metagenomic sequencing data.

claim: EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 symbionts represent the majority of sequence reads obtained from attine ants in field colonies and captive colonies.
source: At the Panama site where we conducted our study, the EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 symbionts are the most common Entomoplasmatales strains associated with attine ants and they represent the majority of sequence reads (>40% jointly for both EntAcro symbionts that were obtained from these ants in field colonies and >50% in captive colonies fed ad libitum; Sapountzis et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous sequencing data.

claim: EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 evolved independently but their gene contents reflect convergent adjustment to life as ant symbionts.
source: We show that these two symbionts are phylogenetically distant and therefore evolved independently (Figure 1), but that their gene contents reflect convergent adjustment to life as ant symbionts when compared to related Mesoplasma and Spiroplasma bacteria associated with other arthropods or plants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenomic and comparative genomic analyses.

claim: Convergences in gene content between EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 primarily relate to carbohydrate metabolism.
source: These convergences primarily relate to carbohydrate metabolism, consistent with patterns of bacterial adaptation being generally based on substrate utilization (Lo et al., 2015; Pál et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on comparative genomic analysis and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: None of the leaf-cutting ant colonies with a high prevalence of Mollicutes symbionts showed any signs of pathogenicity.
source: None of the leaf-cutting ant colonies with a high prevalence of Mollicutes symbionts ever showed any signs of pathogenicity, even when ants had several million Mollicutes cells in their bodies.
evidence: This is an observational claim based on the authors' experience with the colonies.

claim: The combined results suggest that EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 are co-adapted mutualists.
source: Earlier studies left this issue open (Sapountzis et al., 2015; Meirelles et al., 2016), but the combined results of our present study clearly suggest that EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 are co-adapted mutualists and that their metabolic pathways shed novel light on several poorly understood aspects of the highly complex attine fungus-farming symbiosis.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on all the data presented in the study.

claim: The loss of the arginine synthesis pathway in the basal attine ants has been instrumental in making their fungus-farming symbiosis obligate.
source: The loss of the arginine synthesis pathway in the basal attine ants (Nygaard et al., 2011; Suen et al., 2011) has been instrumental in making their fungus-farming symbiosis obligate (Nygaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Outsourcing the production of arginine to fungal cultivars gave complementary efficiency benefits even though it also generated symbiotic dependency.
source: The selection regime that caused this loss remains unknown (Nygaard et al., 2016; Ješovnik et al., 2016), but it is reasonable to assume that outsourcing the production of this most nitrogen-rich amino acid to fungal cultivars gave complementary efficiency benefits even though it also generated symbiotic dependency.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary benefits.

claim: Symbiotic dependency may have created a niche for Mollicutes symbionts to ensure that surplus arginine is recycled as NH3.
source: Symbiotic dependency may thus have created a niche for Mollicutes symbionts to ensure that surplus arginine is recycled as NH3 to provide the most efficient manure for new garden growth.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the evolutionary origin of the symbiosis.

claim: Workers fed with ammonium nitrate transfer nitrogen via their fecal fluid to the fungus garden.
source: This conjecture was recently confirmed for Atta workers in an independent study showing that workers fed with ammonium nitrate (the protonated form of ammonia) transfer nitrogen via their fecal fluid to the fungus garden (Shik et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent independent study.

claim: The only other ant lineage in which Entomoplasmatales endosymbionts have been abundantly found are the army ants.
source: The only other ant lineage in which Entomoplasmatales (Mollicutes) endosymbionts have so far been abundantly found are the army ants (Funaro et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Army ants are exclusive predators of mostly invertebrate prey.
source: These ants are exclusive predators of mostly invertebrate prey (Kronauer, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: 16S rDNA sequences of army ant Mollicutes symbionts suggested they are closely related to EntAcro1 but rather distantly to EntAcro10.
source: 16S rDNA sequences of their Mollicutes symbionts suggested they are closely related to EntAcro1 but rather distantly to EntAcro10 (Funaro et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The Dacetine sister lineage of the fungus-farming ants are also specialized predators.
source: It is intriguing that the Dacetine sister lineage of the fungus-farming ants are also specialized predators (Branstetter et al., 2017; Ward et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Insects hosting Mollicutes symbionts are mostly specialized on nutritionally deficient but protein-rich diets, such as vertebrate blood and pollen/nectar.
source: Broader consideration of the general feeding ecology of all insects hosting Mollicutes symbionts revealed that they are mostly specialized on nutritionally deficient but protein-rich diets, such as vertebrate blood (flies and mosquitoes) and pollen/nectar (bees and flies).
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on comparative analysis of host diets.

claim: Pollen/nectar feeders all had Spiroplasma symbionts with complete arginine catabolism pathways.
source: The pollen/nectar feeders all had Spiroplasma symbionts with complete arginine catabolism pathways, suggesting they might similarly convert excess dietary arginine into NH3, although the absence of functional studies precludes speculation about the type of mutualistic advantage yielded by this conversion (de Groot, 1952; Vrzal et al., 2010; Uchida, 1993; Honeybee Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2006; Nene et al., 2007; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on comparative genomic analysis and is presented as a suggestion.

claim: Primarily non-pathogenic Spiroplasma strains may have been selected to catabolize host-food-associated arginine.
source: Overall, it seems that primarily non-pathogenic Spiroplasma strains may have been selected to catabolize host-food-associated arginine (Figure 5; Supplementary file 3; Supplementary file 4), but this provisional inference needs explicit functional verification by artificial diet experiments and selective removal of symbionts to quantify putative changes in arginine and ammonia titers.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparative genomic analysis that requires further experimental validation.

claim: EntAcro1 was acquired as additional symbiont to EntAcro10 relatively shortly before the leaf-cutting ants evolved.
source: Our results indicate that EntAcro1 was acquired as additional symbiont to EntAcro10 relatively shortly before the leaf-cutting ants evolved and that EntAcro1 supplements already available arginine recycling with novel pathways allowing ant workers to process non-fungal metabolites (Figure 2; Figure 4; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 across attine ants.

claim: Lower attine ants may be generally unable to convert plant-derived citrate or glucose/citrate into acetate because citrate catabolism genes do not exist in EntAcro10.
source: Because citrate catabolism genes do not exist in EntAcro10 the lower attine ants may be generally unable to convert plant-derived citrate or glucose/citrate into acetate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of citrate catabolism genes in EntAcro10.

claim: The acquisition of EntAcro1 likely allowed the ant farmers to tap into additional non-fungal resources to maintain higher metabolic rates.
source: The acquisition of EntAcro1 thus likely allowed the ant farmers to tap into additional non-fungal resources to maintain higher metabolic rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic capabilities of EntAcro1.

claim: A monophyletic crown group of the attine ants evolved in Central/North America following colonization by a single South-American attine ancestor 22–27 MYA.
source: It was recently shown (Branstetter et al., 2017) that a monophyletic crown group of the attine ants evolved in Central/North America following colonization of this subcontinent by a single South-American attine ancestor 22–27 MYA, well before the isthmus of Panama closed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent phylogenetic study.

claim: Most of the higher attine ant radiation happened on a novel subcontinent that was devoid of attine ants.
source: The implication is that most of the higher attine ant radiation happened on a novel subcontinent that was devoid of attine ants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biogeographic history of attine ants.

claim: EntAcro1 may have been domesticated in Central-North America in response to the founding lineage encountering new ecological opportunities.
source: This suggests that EntAcro1 may have been domesticated in Central-North America in response to the founding lineage encountering new ecological opportunities perhaps including plants with EntAcro1-like symbionts.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on biogeographic patterns and the presence of EntAcro1 in T. cornetzi.

claim: Both types of phage-defense systems are likely to have fitness costs.
source: It is increasingly documented that both types of phage-defense systems are likely to have fitness costs (Stern et al., 2010; Vasu and Nagaraja, 2013; Vale et al., 2015; Burstein et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intracellular symbionts rarely have phage defenses compared to gut-lumen symbionts with much higher exposure to phages.
source: Lack of exposure explains why intracellular symbionts rarely have phage defenses compared to gut-lumen symbionts with much higher exposure to phages, which would also explain the presence of these systems in EntAcro1, an abundant gut lumen symbiont (Sapountzis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between symbiont localization and phage exposure.

claim: Preservation by active defense is much more likely to be a naturally selected priority for a vertically transmitted mutualist than for a pathogen.
source: Preservation by active defense is much more likely to be a naturally selected priority for a vertically transmitted mutualist than for a pathogen selected to infect other colonies at the highest possible rate.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference based on evolutionary principles.

claim: Aphids are able to control their intracellular Buchnera symbionts.
source: The endosymbiont-host interactions that we document include several feedback loops that should allow the ants to regulate EntAcro symbiont densities upwards or downwards depending on the overall costs and benefits of their services, similar to other hosts such as aphids which are able to control their intracellular Buchnera symbionts (Wilkinson et al., 2007; Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A study by Gupta et al. (2018) confirmed that EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 have very different origins.
source: A study by Gupta et al. (2018) that came online while our article was in the final stage of proof-checking performed a phylogenomic analysis of 121 conserved protein sequences in 32 Mollicutes genomes, of which some overlapped with the Mollicutes compared in our analyses. The Gupta et al. study complements the results presented in our paper by: 1. Confirming that EntAcro1 and EntAcro10 have very different origins
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an independent study.

claim: The closest relative of EntAcro1 is associated with plants.
source: 3. Confirming that the closest relative of EntAcro1 is associated with plants – in their study a Mesoplasma lactucae isolated from lettuce corroborating the suggestion that the ancestors of the leafcutter ants may have acquired EntAcro1 from plants on which they foraged
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Gupta et al. study.
